title: What is an IPO?
subtitle: The first time a company sells shares to the public
openingQuestion: Why do companies want to IPO?
openingOptions: Because they want to share out their profit
Raise large capital, add liquidity for existing shareholders, boost brand credibility
explanation: An initial public offering takes a company onto the exchange, opening up a large source of capital and creating liquidity for existing shareholders. The cost that comes with it isn't just the underwriting fee: the company must disclose information periodically, bear compliance costs, and most importantly face quarterly performance pressure - which can push management toward decisions that look good this quarter but are bad for the next five years.

diagram.label: A private company needs large capital
IPO: sell shares to the public
Listed on the exchange, early shareholders gain liquidity

realWorldExample.description: VinFast IPO'd on Nasdaq in 2023 through a SPAC merger - an initial valuation of roughly $85B, higher than Ford and GM despite far smaller revenue. The price then dropped sharply - a textbook example of an overvalued, hype-driven IPO.

quiz.question: What does an underwriter do in an IPO?
options: Buys shares on behalf of small retail investors during the initial offering at a guaranteed discount
Manages the shares after the IPO and maintains liquidity on the exchange
The investment bank that underwrites: pricing, selling, committing to buy the remainder
Audits the financial statements before the company is allowed to list
quiz.explanation: Underwriters (Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley...) are paid 3-7% of the total IPO value. They build the book (collect orders), set the price, and under firm-commitment underwriting, commit to buying whatever doesn't sell.

quiz.question: Why do many fast-growing companies choose the traditional IPO route instead of a SPAC merger (like VinFast), even though SPACs are usually faster and initially cheaper?
options: Stricter due diligence, more stable credibility and valuation over the long run
SPACs are always better than traditional IPOs in every listing situation
There is no real difference at all between the two ways of listing
Traditional IPOs don't have to pay underwriter fees, so they're cheaper than SPACs
quiz.explanation: The SPAC (Special Purpose Acquisition Company) route emerged as a faster path to going public, but in practice many companies that listed via SPAC saw sharp price declines afterward due to a lack of rigorous upfront oversight.

quiz.question: What is the biggest cost a company must accept when it IPOs?
options: Underwriting fees, compliance costs, and loss of privacy
A higher corporate income tax rate after listing
A mandatory annual cash dividend to new shareholders
Being required to sell at least half its shares to the public
quiz.explanation: Underwriters typically take 3-7% of the amount raised, plus ongoing audit and periodic disclosure costs afterward. In exchange, the company gets large capital and liquidity for existing shareholders.

quiz.question: Why was a SPAC once appealing to a company without profits yet?
options: Because it isn't subject to any disclosure obligations at all
Because it allows presenting future projections, unlike a traditional IPO
Because a SPAC's underwriting cost is always lower than a regular IPO's fees
Because SPAC shareholders aren't allowed to sell their shares early
quiz.explanation: Traditional IPOs strictly limit presenting forward projections, while a SPAC merger is far more lenient - a big advantage for a company whose story lies in the future rather than in current results.

quiz.question: VinFast's $85 billion valuation at listing, higher than both Ford and GM, says what about valuation?
options: IPO valuations are always independently confirmed by audit beforehand
VinFast's revenue at the time had already surpassed both those companies
The listing price reflects expectations, not current results
Nasdaq sets a minimum valuation floor for electric vehicle companies
quiz.explanation: At the same point in time, the market paid more for a growth story than it did for two manufacturers with far larger revenue. Expectations can adjust themselves very quickly afterward.

keyTakeaways: IPO = the first time shares are sold to the public
**Benefits:** raising large capital, an exit for founders/VCs
Costs: underwriter fees, compliance, loss of privacy

practicePrompt.question: A private (unlisted) company decides to sell shares to the public for the first time on the stock exchange, to raise large capital and increase liquidity for existing shareholders. What is this event called?
options: IPO (Initial Public Offering) = the first time shares are sold to the public - this is the shift from a private company to a public one, allowing large capital to be raised and creating liquidity for the stock
This is called a buyback, because the company is buying back its own shares to increase liquidity for shareholders
This is called M&A, because the company is changing its ownership structure through a transaction with the public
This is simply a bond issuance, unrelated to shares at all
practicePrompt.explanation: IPO = the first time shares are sold to the public. This is the process of moving from a private company to a public one - helping raise large capital to expand the business, while also creating liquidity for founding shareholders and early investors.

summary.keyIdea: IPO = the first time shares are sold to the public
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: **Benefits:** raising large capital, an exit for founders/VCs

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: Pick a Vietnamese company you know that has IPO'd, and try to find out whether the founders/early VCs still hold a large stake - that is exactly the liquidity-exit story you just learned.
application.secondary: No need for exact figures, just enough to see the logic behind the decision.

sections.text: An IPO (Initial Public Offering) is the moment a company first sells shares to the public, shifting from a private business to a listed one - a milestone that can raise anywhere from hundreds of billions to trillions of dong, but comes with no small cost and pressure.
The benefits and costs of an IPO

An IPO lets a company raise large capital from the public to expand its operations, while also creating a liquidity exit for early shareholders such as founders and VC funds that invested at an early stage. In exchange, the company must pay underwriter fees (investment banks that underwrite the offering, such as Goldman Sachs or Morgan Stanley - typically 3-7% of the total IPO value), comply with mandatory disclosure requirements, and bear quarterly earnings pressure from the market - pressure that can push management toward short-term thinking.

VinFast IPO'd on Nasdaq in 2023 via a SPAC merger, with an initial valuation of roughly $85 billion - higher than both Ford and GM despite far smaller revenue, and the share price then dropped sharply. This is a textbook example of an overvalued, hype-driven IPO. A SPAC (Special Purpose Acquisition Company) is a faster and initially less costly route to listing, but it lacks the rigorous due diligence of a traditional investment-bank-led IPO - the market has since learned to price companies listed this way more cautiously.

items: Underwriter: builds the book (collects orders), prices the shares, and under firm-commitment underwriting, commits to buying the shares that don't sell
IPO costs: underwriter fees, legal compliance costs, loss of financial information privacy
Traditional IPO: stricter due diligence, usually creates more stable credibility and valuation over the long run
SPAC merger: faster, but history shows sharp price volatility after listing in many cases

lines: An IPO isn't the destination - it's just the turning point into a new chapter with entirely different expectations and pressures.
